newsitem.title: USA: ADM settles two lawsuits for $65 million.
newsitem.headline: ADM settles two lawsuits for $65 million.

text.p: Archer Daniels Midland Co. agreed Friday to settle two civil lawsuits related to a federal price-fixing investigation for a total of $65 million.
The company agreed to settle a lawsuit alleging that it conspired to fix prices of citric acid for $35 million and another, a class-action filed by shareholders, for $30 million.
Although it agreed to pay monetary damanges to settle, ADM did not admit to any wrongdoing in either case.

Both cases stemmed from a federal investigation of ADM's involvement in an alleged scheme to fix the prices of lysine, a livestock feed additive, citric acid, and high-fructose corn syrup, a sweetener used in foods and soft drinks.

The shareholder lawsuit had alleged that as a result of the alleged price-fixing schemes, ADM's revenues were inflated and thus shareholders had paid inflated prices for the company's stock. The class action suit was being heard in U.S. District Court for the Central District of Illinois.
Details of the citric acid case, which had been filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, were not immediately available.
As previously reported, the Justice Department is said to be pressing ADM to reach a settlement in its criminal investigations of the allegations.
Last month, the department said two Japanese companies and a U.S. unit of a South Korean company pleaded guilty or no contest to charges that they fixed prices in the worldwide lysine market.
ADM acknowledged on Thursday that the corporation and two of its top executives might be indicted as a result of the investigation.
ADM earler had settled another lawsuit filed by customers who purchased lysine. In that case, which was settled in July, ADM agreed to pay $25 million, also without admitting guilt.
The lawsuits were filed after ADM disclosed in late June 1995 that it had been subpoenaed by federal authorities for testimony and documents as part of the government's probe.

The probe began in 1992 when Mark Whitacre, then-president of ADM's bioproducts division, began working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation to expose what he believed was ADM's involvement in a scheme to fix prices of the feed and food products.
The investigation came to light in June 1995.
A source close to the investigation said ADM's settlment -- albeit with pleas of no contest -- indicates a willingness by the agribusiness giant to put allegations of antitrust behind it.
"They really want to start to get this behind them," the source said.

No charges have been filed as yet in the federal probe, although sources close to the investigation say talks between ADM and the Justice Department regarding a possible plea agreement have been continuing.

In its final proxy statement in advance of its October annual meeting, ADM acknowledged that indictments on price-fixing charges are being considered against it and two top executives. Those executives are Michael Andreas, vice chairman and son of Chairman Dwayne Andreas, and Terrance Wilson, a vice president in charge of corn refining operations.
